cues.text: Price goes through your level as if it were not there. No release. No headline. A fast run, then it stops dead and gives half of it back.
You look for a reason, find none, and decide the market knew something. So you chase it, or you fade it because it makes no sense.
Most of those moves make sense once you stop asking what someone thinks, and ask who had to trade.
A dealer re-hedging an options book. A fund resetting its leverage before the close.
A model selling because volatility rose. Stop orders turning into market orders. None of them chose the price. All of them pushed it.
Now, where this sits on your plan. Forced flow belongs to the idea. It sits beside your conviction label, the strong, moderate or thin tag on each branch of your plan, as one note.
It is never a location, a target, a trigger or a direction.
Now, forced and voluntary. Every trade has two sides, but not every side is a decision.
A fund manager sells because the index looks expensive, and can stop when price falls far enough. That is voluntary liquidity. It responds to price.
A holder gets a margin call, the broker’s demand for more money, and sells at whatever price is there. That is forced flow. It does not respond to price.

Voluntary sellers thin out as price falls, so a move into them slows. Forced sellers do not thin out, so a move into them can speed up. It ends when the forced trading is done, not when price reaches anywhere in particular.
You cannot talk a margin call out of selling. It has never once read the room.

The rule: for each idea, name who would be forced to transact if price reached it, and which way their exit would push. If you cannot name anyone, write none known. That is the honest answer most days.
Getting it wrong is fading a fast move because it went too far. It reveals you assume everyone on the other side can be reasoned with. The sellers in that move could not stop at any price.
The fix: the conviction reason on each branch carries one forced-flow clause, a named participant and the direction of their exit, or the words none known. A branch with neither is not finished.

cues.text: When you buy an option, someone sells it to you. Very often that is a dealer, a market maker whose business is quoting prices, not taking a view.
The dealer does not want to win or lose on direction, so they hedge. They hold futures against the options book, so a small move in price leaves them roughly flat.
The catch: the right hedge changes as price moves. So the dealer keeps trading just to stay flat.
Now, the two regimes. A regime, here, is which side dealers are on in aggregate. That side is called gamma.
One: long gamma, dealers net long options. They sell as price rises and buy as it falls. Their forced trading leans against the move, so ranges tend to compress.
Two: short gamma, dealers net short options. They buy as price rises and sell as it falls. Their forced trading goes with the move, so breaks tend to run.
Two slower forces come from the same books. Vanna is how the hedge changes when implied volatility, the volatility the options market is pricing in, changes.
Charm is how the hedge changes as time passes. Both make dealers trade with no move in price.
Options that expire the same day, called zero-D-T-E, carry the most of this in the least time.
Now, the limits. Nobody outside a dealer sees the dealer’s book. Every published gamma figure is an estimate, and vendors publish different numbers for the same session.
Three questions are disputed, with no settled answer.
One: how big zero-D-T-E effects are.
Two: which way dealers must trade as volatility falls, because that depends on who owns which options.
Three: how violent deeply negative gamma days really are. Short gamma can amplify a shock. It does not create one.

The rule: dealer and gamma levels are never locations, targets or if-clauses. No flip, no wall, no key strike goes on your level list. The regime is one word beside your conviction label: long, short or unknown.
Getting it wrong is a call wall written on the level list, or a branch that reads if it loses the flip, short. It reveals that a vendor’s estimate of an invisible book has replaced the auction.

The fix: the regime word lives in one place, the conviction reason. Before 9:25 a.m., check every price on your sheet. Any that came from a gamma source is struck through. Size never moves with the regime.
A wall drawn on a book nobody can see is a guess with a straight edge.

segments.title: The calendar and systematic money
sections: Systematic Money That Trades On Thresholds

cues.text: Some forced flow runs on a timetable. You cannot see its size, but you can know its date, and often its hour.
Start with leveraged funds. A fund like TQQQ promises three times the Nasdaq-100’s return for one day, so it resets its exposure every day.
After an up day, the fund has grown and must buy. After a down day, it must cut and sell. Either way it trades the way the day already moved, mostly late in the session.
Whether that moves price much is disputed. The SEC found some evidence, and called it inconclusive. It is forced. It is not a direction.
Now, the calendar. When an index changes its members, the funds that track it trade the change at the close. The date is announced ahead, so the close is usually orderly.
Add options expiration, month-end, the quarterly roll, and Tier One releases, the scheduled reports that move the market. Each bunches forced orders into a known window.

The rule: calendar events are activity context, never direction. They go on the calendar line of your morning sheet, the one-page plan you write before the session, as nouns only. Expiry Friday. Month-end close. Index rebalance close.
A calendar tells you when the crowd arrives, not which way it is facing.
Getting it wrong is month-end, funds have to buy, so longs only. It turns a timetable into a forecast. The fix: any up, down, long or short on the calendar line is struck through before 9:25 a.m.
And the 3:55 p.m. alarm from Module 17 stays on every day, big close days included.
Now, systematic money. Some funds follow rules, not judgement, and the rules force trades whatever the price.
One: vol-control funds hold more exposure when volatility is low and less when it is high. When it rises, they sell, after the move has started.
Two: CTAs, trend-following funds that trade futures. They buy and sell when price crosses thresholds in their models. Funds do not publish them. Bank desks publish guesses.
The useful idea is the feedback, not the number. A sharp, volatile drop can force more selling later. A long, quiet climb lets both groups add steadily.
The rule: systematic flow is idea-level context, in words. A threshold price from a desk note is never a level, a target or an if-clause.

Getting it wrong is reading CTAs sell below 21,400 and shorting 21,400, with no level, read or trigger there. It reveals someone else’s estimate has replaced your location. The fix: a flow note enters your sheet as words only.

segments.title: Stop cascades and the ladder
sections: First, Second And Third Order, And The Story That Explains Everything

cues.text: The forced flow closest to your chart is stop orders. Stops gather just beyond the obvious places: above a high that has held twice, below a low everyone can see.

A stop is a market order waiting to happen. Price reaches the cluster, the stops fire, and their push can reach the next cluster. That is a stop cascade. It often ends abruptly, once the stops are used up.
Now, trapped traders: people holding positions that price has just moved against.
Price breaks out of a range, and breakout buyers come in.
Then price falls back inside. Those buyers are now wrong, with stops on the far side of the range.
Their exit pushes price further against them.
What that tells you: which way their exit pushes, and roughly where it rests. Below the range for trapped buyers. Above it for trapped sellers.

It does not tell you to trade. A sweep, price running through a cluster, is not a trade on its own. A failed breakout needs the reclaim, price back inside the level, and a trigger. Order flow confirms. It never triggers.
Price is not hunting your stop. It does not know your stop exists. Comforting, and a little insulting.
The rule: name where the trapped side’s stops sit and which way their exit pushes, as context for the read. A cluster is not a location, a target or a trigger. Your own stop stays where you wrote it.

Getting it wrong is fading every sweep the moment it prints, or widening a stop because they hunt the obvious place. The sweep is being used as a trigger. The fix: a blank trigger field means no order.
Now, the ladder. Most traders stop at the first question. Ask two more.
One: first order, what happened. A break of the prior-day high.
Two: second order, who was already positioned for it. Shorts who sold under that high.
Three: third order, who is now forced to transact, and which way their exit pushes.
The risk is the story. Flow stories explain every move after the fact, and explaining feels like knowing. Most forced flow is invisible.
The rule: write the ladder before the session, in at most three short lines. It feeds the conviction reason and nothing else. It is never a reason to exit.

Getting it wrong is rewriting the story to fit each new bar, or holding past the price where your idea is wrong because dealers have to defend this. The fix: write the lines before 9:25 a.m. and leave them. An exit on a flow story alone is logged Too Early.

segments.title: The worked case: one trap
sections: Worked Case: One Trap At The PD High

cues.text: A composite chart, invented prices, built to show the structure of one trap. It stops before any trade. There is no entry and no outcome.
The sheet before the session: the prior-day high zone sits from 21,612 to 21,618. Price is below it, so the far edge is the top, 21,618.
The calendar line says month-end close. Regime: unknown. The forced-flow clause on this branch: none known yet.
Now, 9:30 a.m. Price opens inside value and rotates, testing the zone twice with no 5-minute close above it.
Two groups form. Sellers short under the high, with buy-stops a few points above the zone. Buyers in the middle of the rotation, with stops under the morning low.
Now, 10:22 a.m. First order: price trades through 21,618 to 21,631 in under two minutes.
Second order: the shorts were already positioned against it.
Third order: their buy-stops fire as market orders and push price up through the cluster. The forced buying is spent by 21,631.
Now, the break fails. The 10:24 a.m. bar closes at 21,615, back inside the zone.
At 10:28 a.m., a 1-minute bar closes at 21,609, below the whole zone. That is one close back through, and it completes a failed breakout.
Who is trapped now? The breakout buyers from 21,620 to 21,631. Their stops sit below the zone, from about 21,605 down. Their exit pushes down.
The shorts who covered are flat. They push nothing.
What goes on the plan is one clause: breakout buyers trapped above the prior-day high, exit pushes down.
The regime stays unknown. The conviction label does not change. The prices where forced orders rest, 21,605 and 21,566, are not levels, targets or if-clauses.
The case stops there. Whether anything is entered depends on a reclaim and a trigger at a level, and a stop and size that clear construction. None of that is shown here.
Notice what the case did not contain: no gamma level, no flow figure, no direction written before 10:31 a.m., and no trade. The chart was busy. The plan barely moved.

cues.text: Take your last five written plans. Score one point for each line that is true for every idea on it.
One: who. The conviction reason names a forced participant and the direction of their exit, or says none known.
Two: no flow prices. No price from a gamma chart, a flow note or a CTA estimate sits on the level list, the target line or any if-clause.
Three: regime in one word. Long, short or unknown, inside the conviction reason and nowhere else.
Four: calendar in nouns. Events and times, no direction word.
Five: the ladder, before 9:25 a.m. Written before the session, not edited during it.
Six: stops where written. No stop widened, or placed to dodge an obvious cluster.
Six of six: forced flow is on your plan where it belongs.
Four or five: fix the missing lines before your next session.
Under four: remove every forced-flow word from your plan until lines one to four pass on five plans in a row.
One line overrides the score. If line two fails, treat the plan as under four, whatever the total. A borrowed price is still borrowed, even in your handwriting.
Now, the assignment. Under one idea on your next sheet, write three short lines before 9:25 a.m.
First order: the event, or the break at its level. Second order: who is already positioned there. Third order: who would be forced to trade, and which way their exit pushes.
No prices from any flow source. That is the whole assignment.
Where it goes next. Module 5, The Auction, shows where positions build: balance is where both sides pile in, and its edges are where one side gets trapped.
Module 6 is why no gamma, wall or threshold price goes on your level list. Module 7 is where forced orders print on the footprint.

The forced-flow clause lives in the conviction reason of each branch, written in Module 15. Module 9 builds the thesis it supports. The calendar line is part of the sheet in Module 16, and the close, where the rebalancers trade, is Module 17.
The failed breakout from the worked case is Module 11. The sources for this page, the SEC, ProShares and FTSE Russell, are listed under it.

check.q: Which line overrides the score?
check.why: If line two fails, treat the plan as under four: a price from someone else’s estimate is standing in for a level.

check.q: Your plans score 5 of 6 and line two passes. What do you do?
options: Fix the missing lines before your next session
check.why: Four or five means fix the missing lines. Under four means remove the flow words.

check.q: If a regime appears on your plan, how is it written?
options: As one word in the conviction reason
check.why: Long, short or unknown, inside the conviction reason and nowhere else.

check.q: What does the assignment ask for?
options: A gamma level for the idea
A target from a desk note
Three short lines under one idea, with no flow prices
check.why: First, second and third order, written before 9:25 a.m., with no prices from any flow source.

options: Orders from a participant who must trade regardless of price
questions.why: It does not respond to price, which is what separates it from voluntary liquidity.

questions.q: Which of these may a forced-flow note never be?
options: A clause in the conviction reason
A noun on the calendar line
A line in the post-session mark-up
questions.why: Forced flow is context: never a location, target, trigger or direction.

questions.q: Short-gamma dealers hedge in which way?
questions.why: They buy as price rises and sell as it falls, so their trading goes with the move.

questions.q: Why is a published gamma wall never a level?
options: It sits on the wrong chart
It is an estimate of a book nobody outside the dealer sees
questions.why: Vendors estimate it from assumptions and disagree, so no one can say what would prove it wrong.

questions.q: A leveraged fund resets after a down day. It does what?
questions.why: It trades the way the day already moved, so it sells.

questions.q: Which words are allowed on the calendar line?
questions.why: Nouns only: the event and its time.

questions.q: A sweep prints through a cluster of stops. What turns it into a possible trade?
options: A reclaim and a trigger at a level
questions.why: Order flow confirms; it never triggers.

questions.q: Why is the ladder written before the session and left alone?
options: So the story cannot rewrite itself to fit each new bar
So the size can follow it
So it counts toward the grade
questions.why: A story that changes with every bar has stopped describing the market.
